whyNot: That is pain felt from a body part that no longer exists, after amputation, not pain from an ordinary touch.
Analgesia means reduced pain sensation while normal touch is left intact, the opposite of touch causing pain.
Local anesthesia **blocks** all sensation, both painful and innocuous, rather than making harmless touch hurt.
Nociception is the neural process of detecting noxious stimuli; a bedsheet is not noxious, so this is not the term.
q9-01.why: **Allodynia** means pain from a stimulus that is normally harmless, such as bedsheets on the skin, because sensitized pain circuits misread innocuous touch as noxious.

whyNot: The book calls an **artificial** cutoff such as 1 month inappropriate for defining chronicity.
The book rejects fixed time thresholds; a 6-month cutoff is equally **arbitrary** for this definition.
Chronic pain can be peripheral or central in origin; neuropathic pain is only one type, not the definition.
Many chronic pain states start **centrally** with no peripheral cause, such as fibromyalgia.
q9-02.why: Chronic pain is defined by **persistence beyond what would be expected** for tissue healing, not by a fixed calendar cutoff, which the book calls artificial.

whyNot: The dorsal horn holds the **second**-order neurons, inside the spinal cord, not the primary afferent cell bodies.
The ventral horn is not part of the nociceptive afferent pathway described; primary afferent cell bodies sit outside the spinal cord.
The thalamus is a higher relay on the way to the cortex, not where primary afferent cell bodies lie.
The periaqueductal gray is a site of origin for **descending** inhibition, not primary afferent cell bodies.
q9-03.why: Primary afferent neurons are peripheral, not central, cells: their cell bodies sit in the **dorsal root ganglion** beside the spinal column, outside the CNS.

whyNot: Projection neurons are dorsal horn cells that relay signals up the cord; they are not peripheral sensory fibers.
Aα fibers are not among the three primary afferent types the book describes (Aβ, Aδ, C).
Aδ fibers fall **in between**, sensing noxious mechanical and sub-noxious thermal stimuli, so they are not exclusively noxious.
Aβ fibers detect light touch, vibration and hair movement, responding only to **non-noxious** stimuli.
q9-04.why: **C fibers** end in bare nerve endings that fire only for noxious mechanical, heat or chemical stimuli, making them the true nociceptors among afferent types.

whyNot: NK1 receptors respond to **substance P** in the dorsal horn, not to capsaicin on peripheral terminals.
μ-opioid receptors respond to endorphins and opioid drugs to inhibit transmission, not to cause burning.
Stretch-activated channels make afferents **mechanosensitive**, not capsaicin-sensitive.
5HT3 receptors are excitatory serotonin receptors in the dorsal horn, not the capsaicin target.
q9-05.why: Afferents expressing **VR1** channels are activated by capsaicin and by noxious heat, which explains why both produce the same burning sensation.

whyNot: N-type calcium channels govern presynaptic transmitter release and are the α2δ ligand target, not lidocaine's.
NMDA receptors are glutamate receptors in the dorsal horn, not the target of local anesthetic nerve block.
GABA-A receptors are inhibitory dorsal horn receptors; lidocaine does not act there to stop afferent impulses.
α2 receptors mediate **noradrenergic** descending inhibition, which clonidine mimics, not lidocaine's action.
q9-06.why: Lidocaine blocks **voltage-sensitive sodium channels** on primary afferents, preventing the action potential from travelling to the spinal cord, so impulse flow stops.

whyNot: Spinobulbar tracts reach the brainstem and limbic regions, conveying the **emotional/motivational** component rather than location.
The dorsal column is not the pathway the book assigns to precise location and intensity of pain.
The descending raphe pathway carries **inhibition** downward to the dorsal horn; it is not an ascending pathway.
The corticospinal tract is a motor pathway and is not part of the pain pathways described.
q9-07.why: The spinothalamic tract relays through the thalamus to the somatosensory cortex, the **sensory/discriminatory** route that tells where a stimulus is and how intense.

whyNot: Cholecystokinin acts at CCK-A and CCK-B receptors, not NK receptors.
CGRP acts at its own CGRP receptors, not NK receptors.
Somatostatin acts at its own somatostatin receptor, not NK receptors.
Glycine is an inhibitory transmitter with its own receptor, not an NK ligand.
q9-08.why: The NK receptor family (NK1, NK2, NK3) is activated by the tachykinin **substance P** among the dorsal horn transmitters.

whyNot: Suprasegmental sensitization involves the thalamus and cortex, not the dorsal horn changes seen after amputation.
Phantom pain is classed as a **central** sensitization example, not simple nociceptive pain from tissue damage.
Peripheral sensitization is a separate nerve-level process; phantom pain is the book's example of dorsal horn plasticity.
Placebo analgesia involves endogenous opioid release, which is unrelated to phantom limb pain.
q9-09.why: After amputation, constant firing of the pain pathway causes use-dependent plastic changes in the **dorsal horn**, the hallmark of segmental central sensitization.

whyNot: Demyelination is a structural nerve lesion; fibromyalgia has **no identifiable pathology**, only altered central processing.
The book describes no pathology in muscles or joints for fibromyalgia; the problem is **central** processing.
Fibromyalgia is not attributed to opioid deficiency; opiates are not even proven effective for it.
Segmental sensitization is the dorsal horn type seen with **peripheral** injury, not fibromyalgia.
Gating refers to **closing the pain gate**, where nearby innocuous stimulation reduces pain, not an exaggerated response.
Renewal is not a sensitization process; amplified, prolonged responses after constant input are what **wind-up** describes.
Desensitization is not what happens; constant pain input causes **amplified** responses, not reduced ones.
Analgesia means reduced pain sensation, the opposite of the exaggerated response described.
q9-11.why: Constant firing of the dorsal horn pain pathway causes exaggerated or prolonged responses to noxious input, termed **wind-up**, a feature of segmental central sensitization.

whyNot: NSAIDs reduce input from primary afferents peripherally, which is a drug effect and not what the gate theory addresses.
Opioids sparing touch is explained by Aβ fibers lacking **μ receptors**, not by the gate theory.
The gate theory says nothing about SSRIs; their inconsistent pain effect reflects serotonin's dual actions.
Chronicity is explained by central sensitization, not by the gate theory.
q9-12.why: Stimulating the area near an injury with acupuncture, vibration or rubbing can **close the pain gate**, so innocuous input reduces perceived pain from the injury.

whyNot: The book states fibromyalgia has tenderness without **structural pathology** in joints, so imaging is not diagnostic.
Fibromyalgia has no identifiable pathology, so inflammatory markers are not the basis for diagnosis.
No pathology is identifiable in the muscles, so biopsy is not how it is diagnosed.
Nerve conduction studies are not part of the diagnostic approach; the diagnosis rests on symptoms and pain distribution.
q9-13.why: With no known pathology in muscles or joints, fibromyalgia is diagnosed clinically by counting painful body areas (**WPI**) together with associated symptom severity.

whyNot: The thalamus is linked to pain transmission and to sleep problems, not to concentration difficulty.
The spinal cord is linked to physical fatigue, not to cognitive symptoms.
The amygdala is linked to depressed mood and anxiety, not to concentration.
The hypothalamus is linked to sleep and appetite disturbance, not cognition.
q9-14.why: Problems concentrating, lack of interest and mental fatigue (**fibro-fog**) are matched to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, the hypothesized malfunctioning circuit for executive function.

whyNot: Figure data show gray-matter loss in the thalamus in chronic pain, so it is part of the list.
The DLPFC is among the regions with reported gray-matter loss, so it is not the exception.
Temporal cortex gray-matter loss is reported in chronic pain, so it is included.
One option is the exception: **hippocampal** atrophy is the depression finding, not one of the chronic pain regions.
Blocking VSSCs is how **local anesthetics** work; opioids act at μ-opioid receptors.
Opioids act centrally at spinal and periaqueductal gray μ receptors, so peripheral-only action is not the explanation.
Touch is carried by **Aβ fibers**; C fibers carry noxious input.
μ receptors occur on spinal afferents and the periaqueductal gray, not only the cortex.
q9-16.why: Aβ fibers carry light touch and lack μ-opioid receptors, so opioids dampen pain signaling while leaving normal sensation intact.

whyNot: β1 adrenoceptors are not the receptors the book names for descending inhibition; inhibition acts via **α2**.
5HT3 receptors are excitatory **serotonin** receptors that facilitate, not noradrenergic inhibition.
α1 receptors are not cited in descending pain inhibition; the inhibitory receptor is α2.
D2 receptors are dopamine receptors, unrelated to descending noradrenergic pain inhibition.
q9-17.why: Descending norepinephrine neurons from the locus coeruleus release NE onto inhibitory **α2 adrenoceptors** on afferents, which is why clonidine can relieve pain.

whyNot: The book gives no blood-brain barrier explanation; SSRIs reach the brain and raise **serotonin** there.
SSRIs raise serotonin levels and are not opioid antagonists.
Serotonin does act in the spinal cord, both **inhibiting** and facilitating pain transmission.
SSRIs act on the serotonin transporter; SNRIs add the NET effect, which is the reason SNRIs work better.
q9-18.why: Serotonin inhibits pain via 5HT1B/D but facilitates it via 5HT3, so SSRIs are inconsistent; SNRIs add **norepinephrine** and are proven for pain.

whyNot: The locus coeruleus is the origin of the descending **norepinephrine** pathway.
The substantia nigra is not named as a source of descending pain pathways.
The dorsal root ganglion holds primary afferent cell bodies, not descending serotonin neurons.
The ventral tegmental area is not described as a descending pain pathway origin.
q9-19.why: The descending spinal serotonin pathway begins in the **nucleus raphe magnus** of the rostroventromedial medulla, along with other caudal raphe nuclei.

whyNot: Aβ fibers carry non-noxious touch; overactivity of them is not the hypothesis offered for painful symptoms.
Excess descending inhibition would **reduce** pain perception, the opposite of the hypothesis.
The book does not propose opioid excess; descending opioid release normally reduces pain.
The hypothesis involves normal input that is misperceived, not peripheral nerve damage.
q9-20.why: If descending inhibition is deficient, normally ignored bodily signals from muscles, joints or gut are no longer masked, so they are **perceived as pain**.

whyNot: Duloxetine is an SNRI that boosts monoamines; it is not the antagonist used to reverse placebo analgesia.
Clonidine is an α2 **agonist** that mimics NE inhibition, not an opioid antagonist.
Pregabalin is an α2δ ligand acting on calcium channels, not an opioid antagonist.
Lidocaine blocks sodium channels in peripheral nerves, and has no role in reversing a placebo response.
q9-21.why: Reversal of placebo analgesia by the μ-opioid antagonist **naloxone** implies endogenous opioid release from descending inhibitory neurons.

whyNot: The book says opiates are no better than SNRIs or α2δ ligands for neuropathic pain and unproven in fibromyalgia.
No book statement says opiates work only when combined with SSRIs; SSRIs are themselves inconsistent for pain.
Opiates are **no more** effective than SNRIs for chronic neuropathic pain, so not more effective.
The book names SNRIs and α2δ ligands as proven agents; opiates are not described as approved.
q9-22.why: Opiates work no better than SNRIs or α2δ ligands in chronic neuropathic pain, and in fibromyalgia they have **not been proven** effective.

whyNot: Voltage-sensitive calcium channels are voltage-gated, not ligand-gated, and α2δ ligands bind their α2δ subunit.
These channels are on neurons in the pain pathway, not restricted to muscle.
The channels are **presynaptic**, controlling neurotransmitter release, so postsynaptic-only is wrong.
α2δ ligands bind poorly to the closed conformation, so normal neurotransmission is spared.
q9-23.why: Gabapentin and pregabalin bind best to the **open** channel conformation, giving use-dependent block of the most active, centrally sensitized channels.

whyNot: R-type is not among the channel types named for release in pain pathways; N and P/Q are cited.
Ryanodine receptors are intracellular calcium stores and are not cited as the release mechanism.
T-type channels are not named for release; the book cites N-type and P/Q-type channels.
L-type channels are not named for this release mechanism; N and P/Q are.
q9-24.why: Release of substance P, CGRP and glutamate needs presynaptic depolarization opening **N-type and P/Q-type** voltage-sensitive calcium channels.

whyNot: Peripheral sensitization is a separate process; this question concerns central changes from excessive channel opening.
Excessive transmitter release causes pain, the **opposite** of analgesia.
Muscle weakness is not a consequence the book describes for excessive calcium channel activity.
Loss of sensation is not described; excessive release causes more pain, not less.
Depression is better targeted by **SNRIs**; the α2δ benefit lies in anxiety and sleep.

Fatigue is addressed by SNRIs, sometimes with augmenting agents, not by α2δ ligands.
The book does not list psychosis as a fibromyalgia symptom helped by α2δ ligands.
q9-26.why: Beyond pain, α2δ ligands may ease **anxiety** and improve slow-wave sleep in fibromyalgia, while SNRIs cover mood, fatigue and cognitive symptoms.

whyNot: Cholinesterase inhibition is not how SNRIs affect cognition in the book's explanation.
D2 antagonism is not the mechanism; SNRIs act by blocking reuptake.
SNRIs are not described as increasing GABA for fibro-fog.
